opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it comes down to how research actually works in practice. People imagine you have an idea, you go off, you run the experiment, and you come back with an answer. But it's almost never like that. Most of the time you start with something half-formed, you try it, it doesn't quite work, you look at the results and go, "Hmm, that's strange," and that strangeness is where the interesting stuff is.

So if you have an AI system that just takes a prompt and spits out a paper, that's missing the point. What I'd actually want is something closer to a colleague, someone I can bounce things off. I say, "I think this might work because of X," and it says, "Have you considered Y?" or "Actually, I ran that and here's what happened, and it's weird in this particular way." Then I get to steer. I get to bring my intuition and taste, and it brings speed and breadth, and we go back and forth.

Part of it is that I don't fully trust a completely autonomous loop yet. These systems can go off in a direction that looks productive and is actually a dead end, or they optimise for something that looks like progress on paper but isn't. Having a human in the loop, checking in regularly, keeps it grounded.

But honestly, the bigger reason is that it's just more fun. The joy of research, for me, is that moment of discovery, of being surprised. If I hand everything off and get a finished result, I've lost that. A back-and-forth means I'm still part of the exploration. I'm still learning something, and hopefully the system is too, in some sense. That's the kind of collaboration I find exciting, rather than just automation for its own sake.

r001.rationale: Calling the starting idea “half-formed” does not clearly state that the researcher cannot fully articulate what they want.

r002.rationale: The response says the researcher can “steer” during the back-and-forth after sharing an initial idea, conveying direction-setting toward the intended research.

r003.rationale: The response mentions intuition and taste, but does not connect accumulated understanding of how the idea developed to taking creative, intuitive steps.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that most of the research I've done that actually mattered didn't come out of me sitting alone with a whiteboard. It came out of conversations. The transformer paper is the obvious example. That was eight people in a room, in the hallway, over lunch, arguing, half-finishing each other's ideas. Someone says something slightly wrong, someone else corrects it, and the correction turns out to be the interesting thing. That's how research actually happens, and I think people underrate how much of it is social rather than solitary.

So when I think about an AI collaborator, I'm not really thinking about a tool that answers questions. Asking a question and getting an answer is a vending machine. What I want is the thing that happens when you've been talking to a colleague for three weeks and they already know what you've tried, what you're sceptical of, which half-baked idea you keep circling back to. They can say "hang on, that contradicts what you told me on Tuesday." That continuity is where the value is. A single-shot interaction throws all of that away every time.

And there's a more selfish reason, honestly. At Sakana we're a small team, deliberately. You don't have forty people down the corridor to bounce things off. If you can get even a fraction of that intellectual sparring from a system that remembers your context and pushes back on you, that changes what a small group can do. I'd rather have something that disagrees with me and is occasionally wrong than something that's polite and always agrees. The polite one is useless for research.

I'd add one caveat, which is that I'm genuinely unsure how much of this works today versus how much I'm projecting what I want onto it. The interesting experiment is to actually run it and see whether the back-and-forth produces ideas neither of us would have had alone. If it does, that's a pretty big deal. If it doesn't, we've learned something about what collaboration actually requires.

r001.rationale: The response mentions half-baked ideas, but does not say a researcher may be unable to articulate what they want when first presenting an idea.

r002.rationale: It describes ongoing exchange and context-aware pushback, but does not explain that this lets the researcher steer the collaborator toward the direction originally intended.

r003.rationale: It says the collaborator can remember prior attempts and skepticism, but does not connect accumulated understanding of an idea’s development to taking creative, intuitive steps.

astra-6.text:
Because research is rarely a case of asking one question and getting one answer. You have an idea, you try to explain it, and in explaining it you realize there’s a hole in it. Then someone asks a question that makes you look at it differently. That back-and-forth is a huge part of how you make progress.

I’d want an AI collaborator that could stay with that process: understand what we’re trying to do, challenge an assumption, and help us work out what experiment would actually tell us something. And when the experiment doesn’t work, we can come back and say, okay, what did we misunderstand? The useful thing is having that shared context as the idea develops.

r001.rationale: The response says explaining an idea can reveal a hole in it, but does not say the researcher may be unable to fully articulate what they want at first.

r002.rationale: It describes back-and-forth as useful for progress and shared context, but does not say it lets the researcher steer the collaborator toward the originally intended direction.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect accumulated understanding of an idea’s development with taking creative or intuitive steps.

sol-6.1.text:
Because research is a back-and-forth process. You don’t usually have a perfectly formed question that just needs an answer. You’ve got some intuition, you try to explain it, and someone asks a question that makes you realize you haven’t quite thought it through. Then you change the idea.

That’s what I’d want from an AI collaborator: something that can stay with that process, remember what we’ve tried, and challenge my assumptions. Sometimes the useful contribution is, “Hang on, doesn’t that contradict what you said earlier?” Having something that helps you develop the question, as well as work on the answer, could be really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers may begin with an intuition rather than a perfectly formed question and may not have fully thought it through.

r002.rationale: It describes an ongoing process of remembering prior attempts and challenging assumptions, but does not say this lets the researcher steer the collaborator toward the direction originally intended.

r003.rationale: It mentions remembering what has been tried, but does not connect accumulated understanding of an idea’s development to taking creative or intuitive steps.
